title: Apply environmental management practices in poultry production

lessons.title: Litter, manure and keeping the air clean
lessons.html:
Why the environment matters

A poultry farm produces a lot of waste: manure, used litter, dead birds, feathers, wash water and empty containers. If this waste is handled badly, it can pollute rivers and boreholes, bring flies and rats, cause bad smells for neighbours and spread disease. Looking after the environment protects the birds, the workers, the community and the farm's licence to operate.

Litter in the house

Litter is the bedding on the floor, such as wood shavings or sunflower husks. Good litter is dry and loose. Wet litter causes:

  • Ammonia gas, which burns the eyes and lungs of birds and people.
  • Sore feet and breast blisters on the birds.
  • More germs and flies.

To keep litter dry: fix leaking drinkers at once, set drinker height correctly, keep the ventilation working and remove caked wet patches as your supervisor instructs. If your eyes sting when you walk in, report it – the ammonia level is too high.

Removing and storing manure

At the end of a cycle, used litter and manure are taken out. Follow these rules:

  • Load it straight onto trucks or into the covered storage area. Do not leave heaps lying next to the houses.
  • Keep manure heaps away from rivers, dams and boreholes, on a hard or lined surface where possible, so rainwater does not wash it into water.
  • Cover heaps to keep rain off and flies out.
  • Spilt manure on roads must be swept up.

Poultry manure is a valuable fertiliser and is often sold to crop farmers or composted. It must be handled so it does not carry disease to other farms.

Dust

Cleaning out houses creates a lot of dust. Wear the dust mask and eye protection your employer gives you. Dampening the litter lightly, if your farm allows it, reduces dust. Close the house doors on the side facing neighbours' homes while cleaning, if possible.

lessons.title: Dead birds, chemicals and other waste
lessons.html:
Dead birds

Dead birds must be removed from the houses every day. Rotting birds spread disease, attract flies, rats, dogs and jackals, and smell badly.

  1. Pick up dead birds at every house walk. Wear gloves.
  2. Count and record them on the house sheet.
  3. Put them in the closed bin or container provided. Keep the lid closed.
  4. Take them to the farm's disposal point: an incinerator, a lined disposal pit with a lid, a composting system, or a collection service, depending on what the farm uses.
  5. Wash your hands and clean the container.

Never throw dead birds into the veld, a river or the general rubbish. Never take dead or sick birds home to eat or to feed dogs. If many birds die suddenly, tell your supervisor immediately – it could be a serious disease.

Chemicals and their containers

Farms use disinfectants, fly and rat poisons, and medicines. These can harm people, animals and water.

  • Use only the product and amount on the label or as your supervisor instructs.
  • Wear the protective clothing the label requires.
  • Never wash spray equipment or pour leftover chemicals near a river, dam, borehole or drain.
  • Rinse empty containers as the label says, puncture them so they cannot be reused, and keep them in the locked chemical store until collected for safe disposal.
  • Never use an empty chemical container to carry water or food.

Other waste

  • Wash water from cleaning houses contains manure and disinfectant. It should drain to the farm's sump or soakaway, not into streams.
  • Feed bags, plastic and packaging – collect, sort for recycling if the farm recycles, and keep the farm tidy. Do not burn plastic.
  • Broken eggs and egg shells attract flies; put them in closed bins.
  • Used needles and medicine bottles go into the special containers provided, never into general waste.

The National Water Act 36 of 1998 protects South Africa's water resources. Polluting water can lead to serious action against the farm.

lessons.title: Water, energy, pests and good neighbours
lessons.html:
Saving water

South Africa is a dry country, and many farms rely on boreholes. Birds must always have clean water, but water must not be wasted.

  • Fix or report leaking drinkers, pipes and taps immediately.
  • Close taps and hoses after cleaning.
  • Read the water meter each day as instructed and record it. A sudden rise can mean a leak; a sudden drop can mean blocked lines or sick birds.

Saving energy

Electricity for lights, fans, heaters and pumps is a big cost. Load-shedding also means generators use diesel.

  • Switch off lights in stores and offices when not in use, but never change house lighting or ventilation settings yourself.
  • Keep fans and heaters clean so they work well.
  • Keep house doors and curtains closed to keep heat in during brooding.
  • Report damaged insulation and broken curtains.

Flies and rodents

Flies and rats carry disease, damage equipment and eat feed. They also make neighbours angry.

  • Keep litter and manure dry – fly larvae need wet manure.
  • Clean up spilt feed every day and keep feed in closed bins or silos.
  • Cut long grass around the houses so rats have nowhere to hide.
  • Check bait stations as the farm's pest-control plan says. Rat bait is poisonous: keep it in locked bait stations, away from children, pets and birds. Wash hands after handling.

Being a good neighbour

Smell, dust, flies and noise from trucks at night affect people living nearby. Report complaints to your supervisor politely and quickly. Drive slowly on gravel roads to reduce dust. Keep the farm entrance and roads clean.

Your role

Environmental care is everyone's job. If you see a leak, a pollution risk, a dead animal, chemical spill or a pest problem, report it. Small actions every day make a big difference.

Key points

  • Keep litter dry to prevent ammonia, flies and disease.
  • Store manure covered and away from rivers, dams and boreholes.
  • Remove dead birds daily and use only the farm's approved disposal point.
  • Never pour chemicals or wash water into rivers or drains; never reuse chemical containers.
  • Save water and electricity, control flies and rats, and report problems quickly.

quiz.question: What does wet litter in a poultry house cause?

options.text: Ammonia gas, sore feet and more flies

quiz.question: Where should manure heaps be kept?

options.text: Covered and away from rivers, dams and boreholes

quiz.question: What should you do with dead birds you find on your house walk?

options.text: Record them and put them in the closed bin for the approved disposal point
Take them home for the dogs
Leave them until the end of the week

quiz.question: What should you do with an empty chemical container?

options.text: Use it to carry drinking water
Rinse it as the label says, puncture it and store it for safe disposal

quiz.question: The daily water meter reading suddenly drops a lot. What could it mean?

options.text: The lines are blocked or the birds are sick
The weather is cold so it is normal

quiz.question: Fly larvae need wet manure, so keeping litter dry helps control flies.
It is fine to burn plastic feed bags on the farm.
Which actions help control rats and mice? (select all that apply)

options.text: Clean up spilt feed every day
Cut long grass around the houses
Leave rat bait open on the floor
Keep feed in closed bins or silos
